identification.summary: Infy, also called Prince of Persia, is a long-running Iranian-linked espionage group named by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 in 2016 after a malware family called Infy [S5]. Unit 42 traced the operation back about a decade, and SafeBreach later dated activity to 2007 [S5][S1]. The group went quiet publicly after the 2016 takedown, returned in 2017 with a new malware family called Foudre [S7], and was reported as still active in late 2025 and early 2026 [S1][S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Unit 42 (2016) described a campaign running for about a decade [S5]. A secondary summary of SafeBreach research says activity was traced to 2007 [S1]; accounts of the start date differ across vendors.
identification.notes: Aliases seen in sources: Prince of Persia, Foudre (malware family, also used as a group label), Operation Mermaid, APT-C-07 [S2]. Foudre is the downloader and victim profiler; Tonnerre is the second-stage implant [S2]. Microsoft has no mapped name for this group in this record; msName is empty. Not to be confused with other Iranian clusters tracked by Microsoft.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. SafeBreach assesses the group is a state-sponsored actor operated by the Iranian regime [S4]. Unit 42 attributed it to Iran on infrastructure grounds [S5].
attribution.confidence: SafeBreach calls the evidence solid proof of state sponsorship, based on C2 maintenance stopping during Iran's January 2026 national internet shutdown [S4]. This is vendor assessment only; no government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Unit 42 observed numerous Iranian domains on IP addresses neighboring known C2 servers, suggesting a possible Iranian hosting reseller [S5]. About one third of victims in the 2016 sinkhole data were in Iran [S6]. C2 maintenance stopped on 2026-01-08 when Iran imposed a nationwide internet shutdown, and resumed shortly before restrictions eased [S4].

objectives: Long-term surveillance and intelligence collection on individuals, including dissidents and academics, per SafeBreach [S2]. Unit 42 described targeting of governments and businesses of multiple nations as well as Iranian citizens [S5].

regions: Iran (almost one third of victims in 2016 sinkhole data) [S6]
Iraq, Turkey, India, Canada and parts of Europe (2025 SafeBreach report) [S4]
Sweden, Netherlands, Turkey (earlier reporting cited in press) [S2]
targeting.notes: 2016: 456 malware agents on 326 victim systems in 35 countries [S6]. Scale and sector breakdown of 2025 to 2026 victims are not public in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Custom malware lineage: Infy and Infy M (2016) [S5], Foudre (reported 2017, with anti-takeover features to prevent C2 sinkholing) [S7], and Tonnerre second stage [S2]. SafeBreach reported Foudre v34 and Tonnerre v12-18 and v50 builds, with Tonnerre v50 detected in September 2025 [S4]. C2 uses a domain generation algorithm; Tonnerre v50 redirects to a Telegram group and bot, the first Telegram use since 2016, likely replacing FTP exfiltration [S4]. A variant called Tornado v51 supports HTTP and Telegram C2 and generates domains via a new DGA and via fixed names decoded from blockchain data; it is dropped using a one-day WinRAR flaw (likely CVE-2025-8088 or CVE-2025-6218) that places it in the startup folder [S3]. Foudre is believed distributed via phishing email [S2].

campaigns.name: Infy decade-long campaign disclosed
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 publishes the Infy malware family and a decade-long operation against government and industry targets; Infy and fuller-featured Infy M run in parallel.

campaigns.name: Infy C2 takeover and sinkholing
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 gains control of several C2 domains, counting 456 agents on 326 systems in 35 countries, nearly one third of victims in Iran.

campaigns.name: Foudre emerges
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 observes an evolved Infy successor named Foudre in February 2017 with anti-takeover techniques, reported 2017-08-01.

campaigns.name: Tonnerre v50 and Telegram exfiltration
campaigns.summary: SafeBreach detects Tonnerre v50 (September 2025), using a DGA and Telegram group/bot for exfiltration; Foudre v34 also reported.

campaigns.name: SafeBreach publishes resurgence report
campaigns.summary: SafeBreach publishes its first report on 2025-12-18 describing the renewed tooling and victims in Iran, Iraq, Turkey, India, Canada and Europe.

campaigns.name: Infrastructure churn, Tornado v51, Iran shutdown
campaigns.summary: Between 2025-12-19 and 2026-01-08 the group replaced its Telegram user and all C2 servers and fielded Tornado v51; C2 maintenance stopped 2026-01-08 during Iran's internet shutdown, and new C2 appeared 2026-01-26, a day before restrictions eased.

diamond.adversary: Iran-linked, assessed by SafeBreach as state-sponsored [S4].
diamond.capability: Foudre, Tonnerre and Tornado malware; DGA C2; Telegram C2/exfiltration; phishing delivery; one-day WinRAR exploit [S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: DGA-generated C2 domains, blockchain-derived fixed domains, Telegram bot and group, historically a possible Iranian hosting reseller [S3][S4][S5].
diamond.victim: Dissidents, academics and individuals in Iran, Iraq, Turkey, India, Canada and Europe [S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Surveillance of individuals of interest to the Iranian state, with operations paused when the state shut down national internet access [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, users opening archives with vulnerable WinRAR, and unmonitored outbound Telegram traffic [S3][S4].

gaps: I could not open the primary reports (SafeBreach, Unit 42, The Hacker News) with WebFetch; DNS resolution failed. Details come from search-result summaries and should be checked against the primary pages.
Start date is disputed across vendors (about 2004, 2007, or early 2013 in the imported Citizen Lab text); no reconciliation found.
RSA-based C2 validation is claimed only by a third-party summary (Aviatrix) and is not included here.
Search summaries differ on the date activity resumed (2026-01-26 vs early February 2026).
Initial access details for 2025 victims, victim counts, and any named Iranian government organization are not public in gathered sources.
Citizen Lab/Guarnieri paper (listed in imported references) could not be confirmed in search.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft name confirmed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the individual endpoint and personal communications, especially Windows systems used by dissidents, academics and diaspora, plus Telegram as a C2 channel [S2][S4]. STEP 2: The actor is selective and long-lived, rebuilds after exposure, and is tied to Iranian national network conditions [S4][S7]. STEP 3: Template is phishing or a booby-trapped archive exploiting a recent WinRAR flaw, Foudre profiling, then Tonnerre or Tornado collection and exfiltration over FTP or Telegram, with DGA C2 [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume surveillance of individuals, with rapid C2 rotation after any public exposure [S3][S4]. MDCOA is expansion to US or coalition-linked personnel or contractors using the same delivery chain. Candidate indicators: Telegram bot traffic from non-messaging hosts, DGA-pattern domain lookups, files extracted by WinRAR into startup folders, and Foudre/Tonnerre artifacts [S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reporting for new Foudre/Tonnerre/Tornado versions; activity correlates with Iranian national internet status, which may serve as an indicator of state tasking [S4]. (2) Authorities: this actor mainly targets individuals, so defensive action on personal devices is outside DoD authority; coordinate with law enforcement and the intelligence community for any DoD-affiliated victims. (3) Mission assurance: patch WinRAR and similar archive tools and control Telegram egress on government networks [S3][S4]. (4) Coordination: share DGA and C2 indicators with DC3 and partners; note that the actor rebuilt infrastructure after exposure, so indicators age quickly [S4][S7].

provenance.importedSummary: Infy is a group of suspected Iranian origin. Since early 2013, we have observed activity from a unique threat actor group, which we began to investigate based on increased activities against human right activists in the beginning of 2015. In line5with other research on the campaign, released prior to publication of this document, we have adopted the name “Infy”, which is based on labels used in the infrastructure and its two families of malware agents. Thanks to information we have been able to collect during the course of our research, such as characteristics of the group’s malware and development cycle, our research strongly supports the claim that the Infy group is of Iranian origin and potentially connected to the Iranian state. Amongst a backdrop of other incidents, Infy became one of the most frequently observed agents for attempted malware attacks against Iranian civil society beginning in late 2014, growing in use up to the February 2016 parliamentary election in Iran. After the conclusion of the parliamentary election, the rate of attempted intrusions and new compromises through the Infy agent slowed, but did not end. The trends witnessed in reports from recipients are reinforced through telemetry provided by design failures in more recent versions of the Infy malware.
